name: Tropoflavin

lead: Tropoflavin (7,8-dihydroxyflavone) is a flavone found in small amounts in a few plants and sold as a dietary supplement. It is best known as a small molecule that activates TrkB, the receptor BDNF acts on.
People interested in recovery and brain health use it as a BDNF mimic. The looks connection runs through mood, sleep and motivation supporting consistent training and self-care.

paras: It binds and activates the TrkB receptor, switching on pathways such as AKT-mTOR and MAPK-ERK that are tied to neuronal survival and plasticity, and it is reported to raise neuronal pyridoxal phosphate by inhibiting pyridoxal phosphatase.
Animal studies describe low toxicity with chronic dosing, but human safety data are limited. Flavones in general have low bioavailability. It is sold as a supplement rather than an approved drug.

angle.text: People who use tropoflavin treat it as an over-the-counter way to raise BDNF-type signalling. The appearance link is a chain: steadier mood, energy and sleep support consistent training, diet and skincare habits that show up in how a person looks.

lead: Tropoflavin, also known as 7,8-dihydroxyflavone (7,8-DHF), is a naturally occurring flavone sold as a dietary supplement and studied as a small-molecule agonist of the TrkB receptor, the receptor through which brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) signals.[1] People interested in recovery and brain-and-body resilience use it as a BDNF mimic, with the hoped-for chain running from better mood, motivation and sleep to more consistent training and a better-kept appearance.

The compound is found in small amounts in plants such as Godmania aesculifolia, Tridax procumbens and certain Primula species.[1] Chemically it is a flavone with a catechol group on the A ring (7,8-dihydroxy-2-phenylchromen-4-one).[1] Reviews of flavones note that this family of compounds generally has low solubility and low bioavailability, which has driven work on nanocarrier delivery systems.[2]

Most of the research on tropoflavin comes from animal and cell models, where it has been reported to activate TrkB signalling, support neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity, and influence models of depression, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.[1] Computational studies have also examined it alongside other flavones for antiviral and anticancer targets.[3][4] Its clinical use in humans remains at an early stage, with research focused on prodrug versions that improve stability.[1]

paras: Tropoflavin has the molecular formula C15H10O4. It consists of the flavone backbone, two phenyl rings joined by a pyrone ring, with hydroxyl groups at positions 7 and 8 of the A ring.[1] The plant compounds are made through the phenylpropanoid pathway, and the laboratory compound is produced by multi-step synthesis.[1]
Flavones as a class, including tropoflavin, baicalein, luteolin and chrysin, are noted for low solubility and metabolic processing that limit how much reaches the bloodstream.[2]

Tropoflavin is described as a selective TrkB agonist that crosses the blood-brain barrier and triggers downstream signalling such as the AKT-mTOR and MAPK-ERK pathways.[1] It has also been reported to inhibit pyridoxal phosphatase, raising pyridoxal 5'-phosphate levels in neurons.[1]

Preclinical work reports reversal of learned helplessness and stress-induced behaviours in depression models, improved memory and reduced amyloid accumulation in Alzheimer's models, and protection of dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson's models.[1] Chronic animal treatment has been described as showing low toxicity.[1]

Computational docking studies have tested tropoflavin and related flavones against dengue virus proteins and cancer-related protein targets.[3][4] A 2026 phytochemical study also identified it in extracts of Cestrum auriculatum.[5]
No published human clinical trials were found in the sources reviewed for this article.
